nameStory: Scenedesmus gets its name from the Greek words 'scene' meaning tent and 'desmos' meaning chain or bond, referring to how these tiny algae cells link together like a string of microscopic tents. The species name 'apiculatus' means 'pointed at the tip,' describing the small pointed projections that stick out from some of the cells in each colony.
description: This is a microscopic freshwater algae that you'll never see with the naked eye, but it's incredibly common in New England's ponds, lakes, and slow streams. Under a microscope, it appears as neat rows of 2-8 bright green oval cells lined up side by side like tiny green pills in a blister pack. Each colony is smaller than the period at the end of this sentence, but these little algae are incredibly important as food for water fleas and other tiny aquatic creatures.

idTips.label: Cell arrangement
idTips.description: Cells are arranged in flat, single rows of 2-8 cells that look like green beads strung in a line when viewed under a microscope

idTips.label: Cell shape
idTips.description: Individual cells are oval to egg-shaped with smooth, curved sides and appear bright emerald green

idTips.label: Pointed spines
idTips.description: The outer cells in each colony have small, sharp spine-like projections that stick out from their tips like tiny thorns

idTips.label: Colony size
idTips.description: Entire colonies are microscopic, typically measuring less than 50 micrometers across (about half the width of a human hair)

habitat: Found floating freely in the water column of freshwater ponds, lakes, slow-moving streams, and occasionally temporary pools throughout New England. Prefers nutrient-rich waters and can be particularly abundant in areas with agricultural runoff or natural organic matter. Often found alongside other microscopic algae and plankton in the upper layers of water where sunlight can penetrate.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water temperatures rise and daylight increases. Can be found in spring pond samples but may not yet be at peak abundance.
seasonality.summer: Reaches maximum abundance during warm summer months when there's plenty of sunlight for photosynthesis and nutrients from decomposing organic matter.
seasonality.fall: Still present and often quite numerous in early fall, but populations begin to decline as temperatures drop and daylight decreases.
seasonality.winter: Present but at much lower numbers, surviving as dormant cells or small populations under ice cover in liquid water.

funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, a single drop of pond water can contain thousands of these tiny algae colonies, and they produce so much oxygen through photosynthesis that they help keep fish and other aquatic life breathing - you could say they're microscopic underwater forests!
confusionNotes: Easily confused with its close relative Scenedesmus quadricauda, but that species has longer, more prominent spines on all four corners of the colony, while apiculatus has shorter points only on the outer cells. Think 'apiculatus = pointed tips only on the outside.'
contextualKnowledge: **Note: This identification requires a microscope** - you cannot identify this species in the field with the naked eye. Many people don't realize that the green tinge they see in pond water is often caused by billions of these microscopic algae floating invisibly in every drop.
compareHints: Differs from Scenedesmus quadricauda by having shorter, less prominent spines only on the outer cells rather than long curved spines on all corners. Unlike Scenedesmus obtusus, the cells in apiculatus have pointed projections rather than completely smooth, rounded ends. The spine arrangement is the key feature that separates all the Scenedesmus species from each other.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Scenedesmus quadricauda differs from its relatives by its consistent four-cell colonies and the curved spines on outer cells.
